findings.claim: Nine of the sixteen 12-mark essays (lessons 8, 10, 11, 12 and 13) are set as “‘Statement.’ To what extent is this statement valid? In your answer you should consider ...”
findings.truth: The period study's sixth question is an essay in bullet format built on two identified aspects and answered “with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information”. The quoted-statement, how-far-do-you-agree form belongs to the depth-study essay in the other section of this paper. Lessons 1-7 already use the bullet form; the nine outliers were converted to it and their mark-scheme headings renamed after the two bullets.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, Section A question table (6 compulsory questions, 4/4/8/4/8/12) and the Section B table (essay ... how far do you agree?)

findings.claim: Fourteen 8-mark interpretation questions (lessons 9, 10, 11, 13) are worded “Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation B. In your answer you should refer to Interpretation A and use your own knowledge.”
findings.truth: The task is right for the 8-mark question but the wording is not this board's. This paper asks how convincing an interpretation is, answered from the interpretations and the student's contextual knowledge — the form lessons 1-7 already use. Reworded to match.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1: questions 1-3 are ‘How do interpretations differ?’, ‘Why do interpretations differ?’ and ‘How convincing are interpretations?’

findings.claim: Five 4-mark questions (lessons 9 and 11) are worded “Suggest reasons why Interpretations A and B may differ in their views of ...”
findings.truth: Reworded to the ‘why might the interpretations have different views’ form used in lessons 1-7, with the instruction to use both interpretations and contextual knowledge.

findings.claim: “Specialist vocabulary (sod-buster, dry farming, open range, Big Die-Up) gains marks under SPaG.”
findings.truth: This paper's four spelling, punctuation and grammar marks sit on the depth-study essay in the other section. Nothing in the period study carries SPaG marks, so no vocabulary choice can gain them there.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1: Section A is six compulsory questions worth 40 marks with no SPaG column filled; the 4 SPaG marks fall on the Section B essay

findings.claim: Thirteen invented examiner claims: “the examiner has read the spec” (L1); “The examiner is looking for...” (L2); “this option often pairs...” and “Examiners flag a recurring confusion” (L4); “examiners punish chronologies” (L5); “Examiners reward answers that anchor evaluation” (L6); “Examiners regularly flag a recurring student error on this option” (L7 content_html) and “what examiner reports describe as the difference between a B- and an A-grade response” (L7); “examiners reward answers that split the impact” (L8); “examiners reward answers that engage” (L9); “Examiners reward precise definitions” (L11); “Examiners do not require students to name these historians” (L13 content_html); “the 12-mark band only opens for answers that take a position” (L13); “give the examiner a closing sentence” (L3).
findings.truth: No published examiner report is quoted anywhere, and GCSE History has been graded 9-1 since 2017, so the B-to-A claim is doubly wrong. Each claim was rewritten as plain advice; the two that are actually true were re-sourced to the specification.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1 and 4.4.3; no examiner report cited in any of the thirteen places

findings.claim: “This reframing is now the mainstream view and shapes how examiners reward top-band answers.”
findings.truth: The historiographical point stands; the examiner claim behind it does not. Trimmed to the first clause.

findings.claim: “In July 1845 the editor John O’Sullivan published an article in the New York newspaper the Democratic Review arguing that the United States had ‘the right of our manifest destiny to overspread and to possess the whole of the continent which Providence has given us’.”
findings.truth: That wording is from O'Sullivan's New York Morning News piece of 27 December 1845 on the Oregon question. The July-August 1845 Democratic Review article ‘Annexation’ reads “our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions”. The Democratic Review was also a magazine, not a newspaper.

findings.claim: The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo “added a vast territory — the present-day states of California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and parts of Colorado and Wyoming”, and “in less than five years Polk doubled it again” (repeated in a mark scheme and a flashcard).
findings.truth: The Mexican Cession took in all of California, Nevada and Utah but only most of Arizona and New Mexico; the southern strips of both came with the Gadsden Purchase of 1853. Polk's acquisitions (Texas, Oregon and the Cession) added roughly 1.2 million square miles to a country of about 1.8 million — an increase of about two thirds, not a doubling.

findings.claim: Flashcard 11: “Which historian argued Manifest Destiny ‘dressed up dispossession’?”
findings.truth: The quoted phrase appears only in this unit's own constructed Interpretation 2; it is not Limerick's wording. The question was rewritten so no quotation is put in a named historian's mouth. Her argument in The Legacy of Conquest (1987) is fairly summarised by the card's answer.
findings.evidence: the phrase's only other occurrence is in this lesson's practice question

findings.claim: Four flashcard answers are comma lists: “Religion (Providence), race (Anglo-Saxonism), and republican political confidence”, “The 1837 Panic, soil exhaustion and missionary reports...”, the Mexican Cession state list (L1) and “Lakota Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche (also Crow and Pawnee)” (L4).
findings.truth: List answers fail the validator. Each card was rewritten to one idea; the match sets and key facts in the same lessons still carry the full lists.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: “The first 1846 winter was spent in temporary settlements at Winter Quarters on the Missouri, where roughly 600 died of cold, scurvy and disease” (repeated in a mark scheme and a flashcard).
findings.truth: 359 deaths were recorded at Winter Quarters, and they fall between mid-September 1846 and May 1848 — two winters, not one.

findings.claim: “Tom and Mike on Oregon-bound trails arrived as individuals; Young arrived as a society.”
findings.truth: A drafting artefact: two personal names left in the finished lesson. The sentence means settlers in general.
findings.evidence: internal — no such people appear anywhere else in the unit

findings.claim: “the Mountain Meadows Massacre of 1857 (covered in lesson 13)”
findings.truth: Mountain Meadows is lesson 9 of this unit. Lesson 13 is Little Bighorn and Wounded Knee.

findings.claim: Six flashcards answer with a bare date and nothing else: “24 July 1847.” (L2), “29 November 1864.” (L6), “March 1863.” and “9 April 1865.” (L8), “1847.” (L9), “25 June 1876.” (L13).
findings.truth: A single-token answer teaches nothing beyond the date. Each was given a few words of substance.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: “On 24 January 1848 a Connecticut carpenter named James Marshall...”
findings.truth: James W. Marshall was born in Hopewell Township, New Jersey. He was indeed a carpenter and sawmill operator, and the date is right.

findings.claim: “Within two years California's population had jumped from around 14,000 to over 220,000” by 1850 — repeated in the key fact (“grew fifteenfold by 1850”), a knowledge-check match pair, a flashcard and two mark schemes.
findings.truth: The 1850 federal census recorded 92,597 people in California. The 220,000-250,000 level was reached in 1852. Statehood in 1850 is correct and is kept.

findings.claim: The Donner Party's Hastings Cutoff: “The detour cost three weeks.”
findings.truth: The shortcut delayed the party by about a month and added roughly 150 miles rather than saving 350.

findings.claim: “41 of the 87 died over the winter” (repeated in a flashcard).
findings.truth: Of the 87 members, 48 survived and 39 died.

findings.claim: The Comanche built an empire “that the historian Pekka Hämäläinen has called ‘the dominant power of the southern Plains’”.
findings.truth: The characterisation is fair to his argument in The Comanche Empire (2008) but the quotation marks cannot be sourced to him. Changed to an unquoted paraphrase.
findings.evidence: no located text of that wording in Hämäläinen

findings.claim: “By 1840 ... smallpox — spread by white settlers along the Missouri — had already killed perhaps half the population of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara nations.”
findings.truth: The 1837 epidemic came up-river on the American Fur Company steamboat St Peter's, not with settlers, and it killed at least 93 per cent of the Mandan (about 2,000 people down to a few dozen). About half the Arikara died. ‘Perhaps half’ badly understates the Mandan catastrophe.

findings.claim: “The 1862 Bozeman Trail crossed straight through Lakota hunting grounds...”
findings.truth: John Bozeman and John Jacobs scouted the route in 1863 and Bozeman led the first wagon train over it in 1864.

findings.claim: The congressional inquiry “called it ‘a foul and dastardly massacre’ that had ‘disgraced the very name of an American soldier’.”
findings.truth: The Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War wrote that Chivington “deliberately planned and executed a foul and dastardly massacre which would have disgraced the veriest savage among those who were the victims of his cruelty”. The second quoted phrase is not in the report.

findings.claim: Interpretation 2, ascribed to the 1865 congressional inquiry report: “Colonel Chivington surprised and murdered, in cold blood, an unsuspecting people...”
findings.truth: The report's own wording is “the unsuspecting men, women and children on Sand Creek”. An extract presented as a named report should carry the report's words.

findings.claim: The 1861 Treaty of Fort Wise left the Cheyenne and Arapaho “a small strip in eastern Colorado”.
findings.truth: The reserve lay on the upper Arkansas, in south-eastern Colorado — the ground on which Sand Creek then happened.

findings.claim: “The wealthiest 1,500 families on the Continent — the so-called planter class — held political power in southern state capitals.”
findings.truth: A drafting artefact. The planter class was a Southern elite; ‘the Continent’ makes no sense in an American lesson and reads as leftover text.
findings.evidence: internal — the sentence's own subject is the South

findings.claim: “Women moved into factory and clerical work in unprecedented numbers, with around 200,000 entering the federal civil service or wartime nursing” (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Over 20,000 women volunteered in hospitals across North and South. 200,000 is an order of magnitude out and appears to echo the 200,000 Black soldiers cited later in the same lesson.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Women in the American Civil War’

findings.claim: Sherman's March “and historians widely agree it shortened the war by months”.
findings.truth: No such consensus exists on the march's effect on the war's length. The claim was cut; the aim of the march, which the sentence already states, is enough.
findings.evidence: no cited source for the consensus

findings.claim: “suspicions that the Arkansas party was somehow connected to the killing of a Mormon apostle in Missouri years earlier” (repeated in a mark scheme as ‘anti-Mormon violence in Missouri’).
findings.truth: The apostle was Parley P. Pratt, and he was shot near Van Buren, Arkansas on 13 May 1857 — four months before the massacre, not years, and in Arkansas, which is exactly why an Arkansas wagon train drew suspicion. The wrong state destroys the causal point the sentence is making.

findings.claim: “Brigham Young died in 1877, six months after Lee's execution.”
findings.truth: Lee was shot on 23 March 1877 and Young died on 29 August 1877 — five months.

findings.claim: “Literacy tests, poll taxes and grandfather clauses cut the registered Black vote in Mississippi from around 130,000 in 1880 to under 1,000 by 1900.”
findings.truth: Those are Louisiana's figures and Louisiana's dates: 130,344 registered Black voters in 1896, 5,320 by 1900 and 730 by 1910. Mississippi's 1890 constitution produced a different collapse.

findings.claim: “The second (1870) put federal supervisors over congressional elections.”
findings.truth: The second Enforcement Act was passed in February 1871. Only the first was an 1870 Act.

findings.claim: “Around 1.6 million homestead claims were filed between 1862 and 1900; more than half were abandoned before the five years were up” (repeated in two flashcards and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: 1.6 million is the number of homesteads GRANTED between 1862 and 1934, not claims filed by 1900. About 40 per cent of settlers who began the process obtained title, so roughly three in five failed.

findings.claim: The railroads met “at Promontory Point, Utah”.
findings.truth: The rails were joined at Promontory Summit. Promontory Point is a separate headland on the Great Salt Lake. Both names are given so the lesson still matches the textbooks.
findings.evidence: US National Park Service, Golden Spike

findings.claim: The treaties “assured the nations that the Black Hills would belong to them ‘as long as the grass shall grow’” (repeated in a flashcard).
findings.truth: The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie contains no such phrase. It set the Great Sioux Reservation aside for the ‘absolute and undisturbed use and occupation’ of the Sioux.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868)’, Article II

findings.claim: “In 1874 a US Army expedition led by Colonel George Custer...” (repeated in a flashcard), while the next paragraph calls him Lieutenant Colonel.
findings.truth: Custer's regular-army rank was lieutenant colonel; ‘General’ was a brevet from the Civil War. The lesson should not use two ranks for one man.

findings.claim: “Custer and around 268 of his men were killed.”
findings.truth: 268 is the Seventh Cavalry's total dead and includes Custer, as the lesson's own flashcard says.

findings.claim: Lessons 9, 10, 11 and 13 set only interpretation questions and essays. Lesson 9 has three 8-mark interpretations and three 4-mark ‘why they differ’ questions and nothing else; lessons 10 and 13 have four interpretations and two essays. Lessons 1-7 give one of each of the six question types.
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. Leave it: every set is six questions with legal tariffs, and the missing types are met elsewhere in the unit. Or rebalance lessons 8-13 so each set mirrors the paper, which means writing new ‘describe two features’ and ‘explain the effects’ questions with mark schemes. Recommendation: rebalance in a later build pass, not in this fact-check — it is authoring work, not a correction.
findings.ruling: Question balance in lessons 9-13 (interpretations and essays only) recorded for a later build pass; needs new questions, not corrections.

findings.claim: “Around 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho were killed” at Sand Creek (repeated in two mark schemes and a flashcard).
findings.truth: The figure is genuinely contested. Most reference works put it at about 150; the National Park Service, which runs the massacre site, says around 230, and contemporary estimates ran from 70 to over 600. Recommendation: leave 150, because it is the figure GCSE textbooks use and a student writing it will not be marked wrong — but record the range here.
findings.evidence: US National Park Service, Sand Creek Massacre NHS (‘around 230’); Wikipedia, ‘Sand Creek massacre’ (‘most sources ... around 150’)

findings.claim: “San Francisco's 1851 committee shut down a violent gang in days.”
findings.truth: The Committee of Vigilance sat from June to September 1851 and hanged four men. ‘In days’ compresses months of activity, but the substance — that it acted where courts did not — is right.

findings.claim: Brigham Young “famously said, ‘This is the right place. Drive on.’”
findings.truth: The line is Latter-day Saint tradition, recorded by Wilford Woodruff decades later, not a contemporaneous record. The lesson's ‘famously’ carries enough distance to leave it.

findings.claim: “President Lincoln reviewed the resulting trials and sentenced 38 Dakota men to be hanged.”
findings.truth: A military commission passed the sentences on 303 men; Lincoln reviewed them and approved 39, one of whom was reprieved, leaving 38. ‘Sentenced’ overstates his role slightly. The date, the place and the ‘largest single-day mass execution’ claim are all correct.

findings.claim: “Red Cloud's War is the only war in US history that ended with a Native nation forcing the United States to give up land it had claimed.”
findings.truth: A standard textbook claim and defensible, but a strong absolute. Left as written because it matches the GCSE literature.

findings.claim: Uncle Tom's Cabin “sold 300,000 copies in its first year and 1.5 million in Britain”.
findings.truth: The US figure is right. For Britain the first London edition sold 200,000; the 1.5 million figure covers Britain and its colonies including the many pirated editions. Not wrong, but it needs that qualification if it is ever quoted alone.

findings.claim: The Underground Railroad “helped perhaps 100,000 enslaved people escape ... between 1810 and 1860”.
findings.truth: The usual estimate attaches the 100,000 figure to 1810-1850. The end date is a stretch rather than an error.

findings.claim: Mark scheme: the Dred Scott decision “helped Lincoln's party win control of the House in 1858”.
findings.truth: Republicans won a plurality in the 1858 midterms, not a majority; they organised the House in 1860. ‘Control’ is loose but not misleading at GCSE.

findings.claim: “Around 200,000 Black soldiers served in the Union Army and Navy from 1863, organised into the United States Coloured Troops.”
findings.truth: The official title is the United States Colored Troops (US spelling, as a proper name), and the 200,000 total includes roughly 19,000 Navy sailors who were never part of the USCT.

findings.claim: “Polygamy ... had been publicly admitted in 1852” and a mark scheme's “1852 public announcement of polygamy by Brigham Young”.
findings.truth: The announcement was made by Orson Pratt at a special conference on 29 August 1852, at Young's direction. ‘By Brigham Young’ is shorthand.

findings.claim: The lesson runs to Utah's admission as the 45th state in January 1896.
findings.truth: That is four weeks past the option's 1895 end date, but the spec's bullet is ‘the Mountain Meadow Massacre and its aftermath’, so the settlement is in scope. No label needed.

findings.claim: “The label was a Southern insult borrowed from Scots dialect for a worthless animal.”
findings.truth: The etymology of ‘scalawag’ is disputed; the Scalloway/Shetland cattle derivation is one theory among several. Stated a little too firmly.

findings.claim: Buffalo reduced “to fewer than a thousand by 1885”.
findings.truth: Hornaday's census that found about 1,000 buffalo left in North America was taken in 1889. The southern herd was gone by 1878 and the northern by 1883, so 1885 is close but the sourced figure belongs to 1889.

findings.claim: Every interpretation in the unit is a constructed extract with a generic ascription (‘a school textbook published in 1893’, ‘a 2010 study of US religious freedom’).
findings.truth: None is passed off as the work of a named real historian, and this matches the sibling AQA units, so no change was made. Recorded so the convention is on file.

findings.claim: Flashcard: “Which 1845 event made Manifest Destiny official policy?” — “The annexation of Texas under President James K. Polk.”
findings.truth: Tyler signed the annexation resolution on 1 March 1845, three days before Polk's inauguration; Texas joined the Union on 29 December 1845, under Polk. The card is defensible either way, so it was left.

summary: 13 lessons checked against the AQA specification's assessment section: the period study is six compulsory questions worth 4/4/8/4/8/12, 40 marks, and it carries no spelling, punctuation and grammar marks. Three exam-format breaches drive the edit count. Nine of the sixteen 12-mark essays (lessons 8-13) were set as a quoted statement with 'to what extent is this statement valid', which is the depth-study essay form from the other section, and 19 interpretation questions in lessons 9-13 used another board's wording; lessons 1-7 already used the right forms, so all 28 were converted to match. One exam tip told students that specialist vocabulary 'gains marks under SPaG' in a section that has none. Thirteen invented examiner claims were removed, two of them inside content_html, one citing B and A grades that GCSE History no longer awards. The factual fixes correct James Marshall's home state, California's 1850 population, the Donner Party death toll and the length of the Hastings Cutoff delay, the Winter Quarters death toll, the 1837 smallpox toll among the Mandan, the Bozeman Trail's date, a misquoted congressional report on Sand Creek, the murder of Parley P. Pratt (Arkansas, four months before Mountain Meadows, not Missouri years before), the Louisiana disfranchisement figures given as Mississippi's, the second Enforcement Act's year, the Homestead Act's 1.6 million figure, the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty's wording, and the Mexican Cession's boundaries. Two drafting artefacts were still in the live text: 'Tom and Mike on Oregon-bound trails' and a planter class 'on the Continent'. Two ADJUDICATE items: the Sand Creek death toll (150 vs the Park Service's 230) and the question-type imbalance in lessons 9-13. No lesson is clean.
